pr_title: Fix deadlocks related to ActiveRecord::Migration::CheckPending middleware
pr_body:
### Summary

Fixes #40009

### Other Information

This removes the possibility of deadlocks related to threads trying to gain access to the mutex used in `ActiveRecord::Migration::CheckPending` by removing the mutex and instead having each thread store its own state related to when the migration files were last updated.

The drawback, of course, is that there is some work duplicated between threads. Overall, though, I think this change captures the spirit of the optimization introduced in #37395, but without opening up the potential for deadlocks related to autoloading.

issue_context.title: ActiveRecord::Migration::CheckPending middleware can cause deadlocks when autoloading (using the classic autoloader)
issue_context.body:
### Steps to reproduce

1. Add some code in an initializer that'll be invoked whenever a database connection is checked out of the pool. In my application, it was something like the code that follows. The implementation of `SystemStats` is left out, but the only thing that's important is that `SystemStats` is defined in an autoloaded directory.

```ruby
module DbConnectionPoolStatsReporter
  def self.report(pool)
    pool_stats = pool.stat
    tags = ["spec_name:#{pool.spec.name}"]
    [:size, :connections, :busy, :dead, :idle, :waiting, :checkout_timeout].each do |stat|
      SystemStats.report_gauge stat: "db_connection_pool.#{stat}",
                               value: pool_stats[stat],
                               tags: tags
    end
  end
end

ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::Mysql2Adapter.set_callback :checkout, :after do |conn|
  DbConnectionPoolStatsReporter.report conn.pool
end

ActiveRecord::ConnectionAdapters::Mysql2Adapter.set_callback :checkin, :after do |conn|
  DbConnectionPoolStatsReporter.report conn.pool
end
```

2. Modify a file in an autoloaded directory and make some concurrent web requests

### Expected behavior

All web requests complete as expected

### Actual behavior

Concurrent requests can deadlock. The particular interleaving that causes it to happen is something like this:

```
| Thread A                       | Thread B                                |
|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| gets interlock share lock      |                                         |
|                                | gets interlock share lock               |
|                                | gets CheckPending lock                  |
|                                | tries to autoload SystemStats           |
|                                | tries to upgrade to exclusive interlock |
| tries to get CheckPending lock |                                         |
|                                |                                         |
```

Thread A wants the CheckPending lock, but holds a shared lock on the Interlock, while Thread B wants an exclusive lock on the Interlock, but holds the CheckPending lock. Neither thread can make progress and the server stalls.

This is similar to the deadlock condition described in #34310, just with a different lock. The lock described in that issue was related to database connections, and this one refers to the lock used in the CheckPending middleware introduced in #37395

### System configuration
**Rails version**: 5d3b9f7c8753d74132bf312fdc10356e1d9a0b33 (`master` at the time of reporting). The new CheckPending middleware implementation isn't in a released version of Rails yet.

**Ruby version**: 2.6.1
comments:
I'm not really sure what the right fix is here, but just to brainstorm:

1. Can the `@mutex` be removed safely from the CheckPending middleware? If so, that would allow threads to make progress, allowing concurrent threads to eventually acquire the exclusive interlock.
2. If the `@mutex` in CheckPending can't be removed, maybe it can be made into a `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor` instead, though I'm not sure if that'd help
3. Should users just be dissuaded from adding and code that references autoloaded constants in ActiveRecord connection adapter callbacks?
4. Should we ignore this issue since it's probably not a problem when using zeitwerk?

Hey @cjlarose thanks for the report. Can you make a new application that reproduces this bug? It's easier for us to debug / determine next steps than trying to make sure we're implementing the steps correctly. Thanks!

@eileencodes of course! I've created https://github.com/cjlarose/rails-check-pending-migrations-deadlock, a minimal new Rails app that reliably generates the bug.

When creating the app, I found one additional requirement: `actiontext` has to be disabled. Otherwise, a _different_ deadlock problem rears its head. That deadlock problem is described separately in #36810. (Incidentally, I might have created a reproducible example app for that issue as well.)

So that brings the list of requirements for reproducing the problem to this:

* Use a version of Rails that has the cool new fast implementation of `ActiveRecord::Migration::CheckPending` as introduced in #37395
* Use the classic autoloader (not zeitwerk)
* Disable the use of `actiontext` (just don't load it at all)
* Perform some reference to an autoloaded constant while the mutex in `CheckPending` is held.

@cjlarose Thank you for the application. I was able to reliably reproduce the problem and submitted a fix in https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/40022. It resolves the issue you described locally but it'll be good if you can try out the fix as well in case I missed something.
@tgxworld Thanks for taking a look! I'll leave feedback in the PR itself.
Opened up my own solution to the problem in #40032

As far as I understand it, the classic autoloader isn't threadsafe by default, but with very careful application of tools like the Load Interlock, `LoadInterlockAwareMonitor`, and `permit_concurrent_loads`, it's possible to use the classic autoloader safely in multithreaded environments.

The problem with the `CheckPending` middleware, I think, is that it lacks the appropriate safeguards to make it compatible with the classic autoloader in multithreaded environments. But the tools exist to make it work and are already employed in different parts of Rails. It's just a matter of figuring out what tools we can employ in this particular situation to prevent deadlocks, while keeping the implementation efficient.

review_comments: Why the WeakRef here? Just to avoid having to delete keys from the hash? The size of this cache should not increase with bound given it is direct related to how many threads you use in your webservers.

It's true that in Rails' default puma config, the number of threads is static

```ruby
max_threads_count = ENV.fetch("RAILS_MAX_THREADS") { 5 }
min_threads_count = ENV.fetch("RAILS_MIN_THREADS") { max_threads_count }
threads min_threads_count, max_threads_count
```

But users can use different configurations which allow puma to kill idle threads and spin up new threads on demand

```ruby
threads 1, 5
```

...or they could be using totally different web servers that similarly spin up and spin down threads as necessary.

Without the `WeakRef`s, that would result in a memory leak since the `Thread` objects would never be GC'd.
@rafaelfranca Lemme know if that explanation makes sense. Happy to remove `WeakRef` if it turns out it's not actually beneficial, but I think it might be.
